notions.question: How did John Major govern after Thatcher, and why did he lose in 1997?
notions.definition: John Major succeeded Thatcher in November 1990. He replaced the poll tax with the council tax, took part in the Gulf War (1991) and narrowly won the 1992 general election. On 16 September 1992 ("Black Wednesday"), sterling, under speculative attack, had to leave the European Exchange Rate Mechanism: the Conservatives' economic credibility collapsed, even though growth later returned. The party tore itself apart over the Maastricht Treaty (ratified in 1993, with opt-outs for the United Kingdom on the single currency and the Social Chapter), and the government was weakened by scandals ("sleaze"). Major continued privatisation (coal, railways) and launched the peace process in Northern Ireland (Downing Street Declaration, 1993). Tony Blair's Labour Party won by a wide margin on 1 May 1997.

lignes: Black Wednesday: exit from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism
Ratification of Maastricht; Downing Street Declaration; council tax

notions.titre: New Labour and the Third Way
notions.question: In what ways did Tony Blair's New Labour break with traditional Labourism?
notions.definition: After becoming Labour leader in 1994, Tony Blair modernised the party: Clause IV was rewritten in 1995 (dropping the goal of common ownership of the means of production), a "New Labour" image was adopted and the party distanced itself from the trade unions. The "Third Way", theorised in particular by the sociologist Anthony Giddens, seeks to move beyond the opposition between state socialism and neoliberalism: accepting the market economy and the Thatcherite legacy (no renationalisation), while investing in education, health and getting people into work (welfare to work). After the 1997 victory, the government gave the Bank of England independence over monetary policy (1997), created a national minimum wage (1998), passed the Human Rights Act (1998) and launched devolution. The record is tarnished by the Iraq War (2003). Gordon Brown succeeded Blair in 2007.

lignes: National Minimum Wage Act; Human Rights Act; Good Friday Agreement

termes.definition: A synthesis of market economics and social justice.
A policy encouraging a return to work.

exemple.texte: The slogan "Tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime" can be discussed as an example of the New Labour synthesis of firmness and social action.

confusions.explication: Blair explicitly claimed to break with the old doctrine.

notions.question: How did the United Kingdom transfer powers to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?
notions.definition: Devolution is the transfer of powers from the Westminster Parliament to elected institutions in the constituent nations, without federalism: Westminster remains sovereign. After the referendums of September 1997 (a large "Yes" in Scotland, a narrow "Yes" in Wales), the Scotland Act 1998 created the Scottish Parliament (Holyrood) with wide legislative powers (health, education, justice) and tax-raising powers; the Government of Wales Act 1998 created a Welsh Assembly, initially with limited powers, since extended (Senedd). The Northern Ireland Act 1998 set up a power-sharing Assembly arising from the Good Friday Agreement. Devolution raises the "West Lothian question" (Scottish MPs vote at Westminster on laws that concern only England) and has not extinguished Scottish nationalism (2014 independence referendum: 55% "No").

termes.definition: The transfer of powers to regional institutions.
Non-English MPs voting on English matters.

exemple.texte: Free university tuition for Scottish students in Scotland, unlike the English system, illustrates the Scottish Parliament's capacity to pursue its own policies.

confusions.explication: The United Kingdom remains a unitary state.

notions.question: How did the Good Friday Agreement bring the "Troubles" in Northern Ireland to an end?
notions.definition: The Northern Ireland conflict ("the Troubles", late 1960s - 1998) mainly pitted republicans / nationalists, mostly Catholic and in favour of unification with Ireland, against unionists / loyalists, mostly Protestant and attached to the United Kingdom; it claimed more than 3,500 lives. The Good Friday Agreement (or Belfast Agreement), signed on 10 April 1998 by the British and Irish governments and most of the Northern Ireland parties, was approved by referendum in the North and in the Republic of Ireland on 22 May 1998. It provides for: the principle of consent (Northern Ireland remains British for as long as a majority wishes), a power-sharing Assembly and Executive between the communities, North-South and East-West cooperation bodies, the amendment of Articles 2 and 3 of the Irish Constitution, the disarmament of paramilitary groups and the early release of prisoners. The question of the Irish border was at the heart of the Brexit negotiations.

flashcards.question: Trace the period 1990-2007: Major, New Labour, devolution, the Good Friday Agreement.
flashcards.reponse: Major (1990-1997): council tax, 1992 victory, Black Wednesday (16 September 1992), divisions over Maastricht, sleaze, rail privatisation, Downing Street Declaration (1993). New Labour: Clause IV rewritten (1995), Third Way (Giddens), victory on 1 May 1997, Bank of England independence, minimum wage and Human Rights Act (1998), Iraq (2003), Brown (2007). Devolution: 1997 referendums, Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly (1999), unitary state, West Lothian question, 2014 Scottish referendum (55% No). Good Friday (10 April 1998, referendums on 22 May): consent, power-sharing, North-South bodies, decommissioning.
